peigneur.text: Imagine working on an oil rig... when the entire lake beneath you starts disappearing.
The water begins to spin. And the rig starts to tilt.
This is Lake Peigneur, in Louisiana. November twentieth, nineteen eighty.
The lake was only ten feet deep. But beneath it was a giant salt mine.
That morning, an oil drill got stuck more than twelve hundred feet down.
It had punched straight into the mine.
Water poured in, dissolving the salt pillars that held the tunnels up.
The hole grew wider... and the lake drained, like a giant bathtub.
A whirlpool swallowed the rig, a tugboat, eleven barges, and part of an island.
Even a nearby canal flowed backwards, into a hundred-and-sixty-foot waterfall.
All seven men on the rig escaped. So did all fifty-five miners.
Nobody was killed. But when the lake refilled... it was salt water.

molasses.text: Imagine walking down the street... when a giant wave of thick, sticky liquid comes rushing toward you.

molasses.text: On the waterfront stood a fifty-foot steel tank, holding over two million gallons of molasses.
It leaked so badly, it was painted brown to hide the stains.
Then the rivets started popping, like gunfire... and the tank burst apart.
A wave up to twenty-five feet high tore through the streets at around thirty-five miles an hour.
It crushed buildings, and twisted the steel of an elevated railway.
And here's what made it so deadly. In the freezing air, the molasses thickened like glue.
Anyone caught in it couldn't escape.
Sailors, police and Red Cross nurses waded in to help.
Twenty-one people died. About a hundred and fifty were injured.
It sounds unbelievable. But it was real... and it changed building safety rules for good.

sinkhole.text: Imagine falling asleep in your own bed... and the ground beneath your bedroom opens up.
Seffner, Florida. February twenty-eighth, twenty thirteen. Around eleven at night.
The family was getting ready for bed, when a loud crash rang out.
Jeremy Bush ran to his brother Jeff's bedroom... and the room was gone.
Jeff, and everything in his room, had dropped into a hole thirty feet wide.
Jeremy jumped in, digging desperately, calling his brother's name.
But the floor kept collapsing. A sheriff's deputy reached in, and pulled him out.
So how does the ground just... vanish?
Much of Florida sits on limestone, and rainwater slowly eats it away, leaving hidden caverns.
The soil above can hold... until suddenly, it can't.
Rescuers searched, but the ground was too unstable. Jeff's body was never recovered.
And here's the haunting part. That same sinkhole has opened up again. Twice.
